entities.name: Communist Party of India
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Communist Party of India (CPI), founded in 1920 in Tashkent (Soviet Central Asia) by M.N. Roy as the first communist party in Asia outside the Soviet sphere, was the dominant left-wing force in Indian politics from the 1940s through the 1960s before fragmenting into multiple communist parties. The CPI's role in the Indian independence movement, its government in Kerala (1957 — the world's first democratically elected communist government), and its complex relationship with the Indian National Congress shaped independent India's political landscape.

M.N. Roy (Manabendra Nath Roy), one of the founders of the Communist International who debated Lenin on colonial policy, founded the CPI in Tashkent. The party grew primarily in Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala, where it organized peasants and industrial workers. During World War II, the CPI controversially supported the British war effort (after the Soviet Union entered the war) against the Indian National Congress's Quit India movement — creating lasting credibility damage.

The CPI's 1957 Kerala election victory under E.M.S. Namboodiripad — creating the world's first democratically elected communist government — was dismissed by India's central government (Nehru's Congress) after 28 months under Article 356. The party's 1964 split into CPI and CPI(M) (Marxist) following the Sino-Soviet split reflected the global communist fragmentation. CPI(M) subsequently governed West Bengal continuously from 1977-2011 (34 years — world's longest continuous elected left-wing government) and Kerala multiple times.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Communist Party of India's 1957 Kerala government — the world's first democratically elected communist government — demonstrated that communism could win power through the ballot box rather than revolution, reshaping global communist political strategy.
